Brilliant game, the concept of reviewing criminal cases by only listening to audio recordings is very unique. Each case had kept me interested and wanting to know more. No case felt like a chore in the play through. However the game is pretty short and once you solved the cases there really is no need to replay other than trying to unlock all the achievements. I really hope in the future there will be plans to add more cases to solve. 

Overall, i would give this game a 8/10
Possibly the purest "detective simulator" I've ever played. No hints, no markers, no automatically made deductions. It's just you and the raw evidence.

[i]Unheard[/i] is basically a combination of [i]The Case of the Golden Idol[/i] and [i]Telling Lies[/i]. You play as a detective wired to an experimental machine that allows you to listen to all conversations of various people in different rooms in a building. Your goal in each case is to follow them around, collecting information and context, and answer a series of questions about the whole thing (like who the culprit is).

The detective aspect of the game is less compelling than [i]The Case of the Golden Idol[/i] or [i]Return to Obra Dinn[/i]. You do have to connect some dots sometimes, but often characters just spell everything out and admit their wrongdoings — you just need to find them. The dialogues themselves are terribly overacted and unnatural.

Moreover, the game suffers from the same issue [i]Telling Lies[/i] did: downtime. There is a decent fast forward button, but you still spend too much time just waiting for a person to do something or listening to the pauses on one end of a conversation.

The final case, which makes you figure out which patiens of a mental asylum are insane and which are pretending is by far the most fun one. Some players will probably find the ending annoying, but I think it fits perfectly — such are the genre expectations!

All in all, I don't think it's the best whoddunit game ever, but I respect all developers trying new approaches to detective games. It's short, too, which in this case is a boon as the gameplay does become stale with time. If you're interested in detective stories, this one may be worth checking out.

P. S. And what's up with the insane number of sales? Don't get me wrong, I'm all for indies achieving success, but this game, while worth some attention, is not a mindblowing gem. I wonder how it won over so many people.

I love detective games. I enjoy the challenge of cracking a case. Detective games don’t need to be long -- the story just needs to be good, and the mystery engaging. Needless to say then that [I]Unheard[/I] is an appealing game to me from the start, and it is a fun, innovative one as well.
 
Some detective games include a mechanic (or gimmick) or two that differentiate themselves from the others, making the case-solving more interesting. [I]L.A. Noire[/I] requires you to examine your suspects’ facial expressions; [I]Her Story[/I] involves unearthing video clips using keywords to slowly piece together the actual narrative; [I]Orwell[/I] has you make decisions about conflicting evidence that can alter how the story unfolds. The hook in [I]Unheard[/I] is that you investigate crime scenes by just listening to conversations and ambient sounds.
 
While you can move around a crime scene virtually, you as the character are not actually on location. You will pick up different audio clues depending on where you are during the duration of the crime. That means you will need to replay the crime scene audio clip multiple times to gather all the clues, before making your final conclusions. Thankfully, the vocal performances are distinctive enough, albeit rather exaggerated at times like in a radio play, for you to keep track of who are talking at different times.
 
Each case gets more complicated and challenging by introducing more characters and concurrent conversations. You can keep track of the happenings by adding notes at a particular timestamp, a feature of which I made excessive use. I did not find [I]Unheard[/I] to be a difficult game, and that did not make this game any less enjoyable. As long as you are thorough with your investigation, I believe you can solve each case without making any mistakes. I found it quite satisfying to be able to solve the cases without assistance just by being attentive and methodical.
 
Playing thoroughly and thoughtfully got me almost 8 hours of gameplay, so I consider [I]Unheard[/I] to be of great value. At the time of this review (updated November 2019), there are 2 free DLCs available. The one called [I]The Lethal Script[/I] is presented in both English and Mandarin Chinese, but the other in Mandarin Chinese only. These DLCs can only add to the [I]Unheard[/I] experience.

Because of the game’s reliance on audio clues, thus the absence of subtitles, players who are deaf and hard of hearing will not be able to enjoy it. I hope the developer can eventually find a way to circumvent this because [I]Unheard[/I] is truly a gem in the indie game scene that fans of detective games should check out.

[h1]Regular Review[/h1]
To get mandatory comparison to [b]Obra Dinn[/b] out of the way: no, [b]Unheard[/b] doesn't reach the heights of Lucas Pope's masterpiece aesthetically, narratively or gameplayfully (this is a real adjective that I found in a dictionary of real adjectives). 

Is it still an enjoyable detective game though? Sure.

[b]Unheard[/b]'s gameplay is entirely audio-based. Each case is a bit of detective mystery radio drama simultaneously playing out across multiple rooms. Player "character" moves around unseen, listening in on conversations, but only in a single room at a time. Gather enough clues, pinpoint the speakers' identity, figure out the mystery, move on to the next level. It's a satisfying core mechanic testing player's deduction and attention. 

The game's quite short - around 4 hours. It feels a tad like a proof of concept: once the game really gets going, and cases get complicated and challenging enough, [b]Unheard[/b] ends. There is, however, an upcoming free dlc that will, hopefully, explore the acoustic detective mechanic to its full potential.
On the other hand, like a well-paced mystery novel, the game doesn't overstay its welcome. Five cases cleverly build up to an ambiguous story arc conclusion.
Voice acting is fairly competent. Occasionally feels cheesy with cliche accents, but I suppose it might be necessary for keeping a score of character voices easily distinguishable.

[b]Unheard[/b] definitely succeeds at making the player feel like they're doing a real detective job. Trust me, I'm a real imaginary detective.

[h1]Daft Review[/h1]
Greetings, fellow eavesdroppers!
Your family, neighbours and colleagues keep on having dull conversations entirely unworthy of listening in on? Everything they talk about is disgustingly mundane? 
Your spouse never conspires against the authorities behind closed doors?
Your boss doesn't run a blackmailing ring?
Even your neighbour's dog is an exemplary good boy, all cheerful bark and no murderous scheme?
I get your disappointment! Luckily, [b]Unheard[/b] is here to provide a cast of mischievous bastards for your eavesdropping needs! Assassination plots, robbery plans, fancy backstabbing - it got you covered. What a lovely feast of a noble art of eavesdropping! Listen away!

Really good. Easily recommended to who like playing detective games. Its my first time dealing with games that we have to solve with purely auditory clues.

You really feels the clueless-ness when starting a new case. Gaining a new perspective every time replaying the scenes will never get old.  The story is while needed some sort of suspension of disbelief, are written spectacularly. I got windblown every time multiple time in my play through.

My favorite thing is when advancing through the campaign you started to see that there are a lot of lines interconnected.
While at first you might question a lot of things like why I'm in this room, is this some sort of interview or a test? What for? 
The very inquisitive nature of player will get rewarded as all detective games should be is what the best thing this game offers to me.

Easily recommended. Get the DLC too while you at it. Its completely free, another plus point that I can give to this already wonderful game.

Unheard is very less complicated puzzle game, where the mechanics just involves the player solving mysteries but with a twist of course. You can revisit the past and listen to what the victims/witnesses/perpetrators are saying and then you use the information to solve the questions asked by the game.  The core creative concept of the game is ingenious, it is one of a kind which I have ever played in. Most mysteries are inspired by various short stories and novels by other authors but the freshness of new ideas of the devs promotes the game more than anything. 

[b] Story [/b] 
There are several mysteries and stories for you to solve in the main game, even though they does seem separate there seems to be an interconnection. You are an employee for a new experiment which helps the forces to solve crimes, and it seems you are guinea pig. You have no face no name, you can't see the face of the person in front of you, everything is in anonymous but the story weaves the connection. Who are you exactly? Why are you here? These are the questions the game will make you ponder for hours.  My favorite one is the mental hospital scenario and the one at the police station, they were interesting. 

[b] Gameplay [/b]
Gameplay is pretty basic, you have the audio track playing, you can reverse the track, keep notes, fast forward the track. Along with the track there is a map for each scenario and you can see the characters, you cannot interfere with them because you are the listener and the listener only. You can follow them at a time and listen to what they say. This is how you gain the main clues and info to solve the mysteries. I liked the simplicity of it. 

[b] Voice Acting [/b]
Voice acting is super super good in the game, it was very well done af. Kudos to the voice actor team. If it was not voiced, I doubt the game is this good (or purposeful lol) 

[b] DLC [/b]
There is an english dubbed/subbed DLC available and that is probably one of the hardest mysteries and the longest one there is. If you solve that one you are a true hero and I'd love to be friends with you haha. I will shamefully say that I got help in that one, I was very close to the real answer tho. It was waaaay thinking out of the box and I'm not that smart. There is also another DLC which is in chinese and I feel like more interesting af as well, sadly waiting for it to be subbed. If it's a funds problem I will gladly support the devs in order to get the subbed version tbh. Really love to play that. 

[b]Overall[/b] 
It's a very neat puzzle mystery game of the crime genre with plot twists both in gameplay and the story, certain scenarios could be sensitive to some individuals so please check before buying.

I love the idea of this, I really do, and I really want to play this and enjoy it. However, the lack of subtitles is what's barring me from enjoyment. I have auditory processing issues and I typically require subtitles in most dialogue heavy games, so the lack of them in this game breaks my heart. I unfortunately cannot play the game because of this, and I hope to see subtitles in the future. Stay away if you're like me and you need subtitles to function in dialogue heavy games!

Some important context for this review: [b]I was mislead by the screenshots into buying this game[/b] - they make it look like there are subtitles, like "hearing" is actually [i]reading[/i]. It is not. It is [b]hearing[/b] sound, with your [b]ears[/b].

Furthermore, I'm not technically hearing impaired but have significant difficulty discerning words (I have to watch TV with subtitles or I literally can't understand the dialogue). However, I have little trouble with audiobooks because the voices are so clear, the audio quality so high, and there are zero other sounds to muddy the waters.

With all of that in mind, consider that I completed the first three puzzles. It was a struggle, but I did it.

The first was effortless.

For the second puzzle, I got all of the names but had missed two very important details because of the sheer amount of background noise. I eventually had to look it up because I felt like I was going crazy. No, I just [i]literally couldn't hear[/i] the answer to the puzzle.

The third puzzle, I got all on my own - but was nearly fucking [b]deafened[/b] by the explosion. That's not hyperbole, I had to turn the audio up so much to hear a conversation, and this game outright tells you to use headphones, that it made my ears ring. I almost quit right then. It's worth noting that there were actually a couple of conversations I couldn't hear, I just made some assumptions based on the other details I did know.

I should have quit at the explosion. I should have, in fact, quit as soon as I was struggling to hear dialogue over background noise that [i]physically hurt my ears[/i] to listen to.

I'm quitting now because I'm tired of struggling to hear, tired of the pain in my ears, and tired of playing a game that feels like [i]work[/i]. It's the most exhausting game I've ever played.

[b]TL;DR: Don't buy unless your hearing is 100% absolutely perfect, and your ears aren't hurt by high pitched sounds[/b]

In [b]Unheard[/b], you need only listen to what the characters are saying. You are allowed the choice of going back and forth between the audio and listening to it as many times as you want. There is no time limit and listening to all the details is crucial for you to solving the case. Characters and storylines intermix. It’s up to you to figure out in what order these events took place, who was where, who is doing what, and who is still relevant just cause. The cases are engaging, the voice acting does the game so much justice to bring the characters to life and its plot twist after plot twist. 

Some of the cases start to get longer and audio times reach up to about 15 minutes in length. [b]Unheard[/b] is original, the design intriguing, and the writing captivating.  [b]Unheard[/b] has a lot of potential and the studio is planning on releasing additional free DLC in the near future. The only con to the game is that it’s a bit short, but it’s still enough to keep you engaged by the mysteriousness of it all at a good pace.

I discovered [i]Unheard[/i] while looking through every deduction game on Steam, like a raccoon looking through a dumpster for a half-eaten cake. It is an audio-based deduction game wherein you are given a top-down blueprint view of a building, and a scrubber (like a YouTube playback bar) that allows you to play out 10-20 minutes worth of story. You can only hear audio near where you are standing, so to put together what's going on, you need to walk around, scrub around, and replay segments, following different speakers. There are limited quality of life features, but it does feel a bit like a chore, and trying to find all the audio will require long periods of fast forwarding through silence. You are then asked to identify who each speaker is and answer some questions about a crime. The main game is 5 cases, and there are 3 DLC cases (two of which are Chinese-only).

I didn't like this game at all! The individual cases are quite simple, but have very low informational density, so you need to play out very long scenes only to learn very little. The real-time conversation mechanic plays a lot better in [i]Tacoma[/i] or [i]The Invisible Hours[/i], though neither have explicit deduction mechanics. The writing is atrocious. This is 50% because the dialogue is Chinese-first (the worst example: a guy is mad that someone keeps hanging up on him on the phone and I think he's meant to say "What's the deal?" or "What the hell?" but he says "WHAT'S THE CHECKOUT???"). But it's also 50% because the dialogue is written to have people deliberately obfuscate what they're saying to try to create a plausible puzzle. The voice direction is also very poor. The voice actors do seem to be native English speakers but not professional actors. This is at its worst in the first few cases. There's one part where two actors are smoking and the foley noise for the smoking is just someone breathing weird. So bad. The game also uses very grating sound effects for explosions, phones ringing, and occasionally weird creepy ASMR echo noises. These add nothing and take away a lot.

The game also doesn't have subtitles. The typical defence here is that the puzzle is trying to figure out what's being said. But that's not the puzzle. Absolutely no case in the game involves trying to make out ambiguous speech. Individual speakers have equalizers as they speak, so there's also no confusion about who is saying something. I think if you build an audio puzzle that does not have any kind of subtitle or text cue, it needs to be the case that the puzzle is ABOUT the audio, not using audio to deliver information that could easily be textual. I have no idea why the game tells you it works better with headphones.

The game superficially appears to be about you being a detective and learning to use this "ADS" system to solve cases, but the frame story unfolds to very clunkily claim you're an escaped mental patient using this technology as an experimental ego-death therapy. This is beyond stupid. 

One sin a lot of deduction puzzle games commit is making the puzzle just be about finding a key, rather than actually deducing anything. So, if a conversation has John tell Mark "Hi Mark, how are you doing?", filling in "Mark" as the other guy's name is using a key -- you immediately know to put it in the lock -- not deducing something. On the other hand, if the scene features two women, the name list has two female names, and only one woman is identified, identifying the other is a deduction. You do need to provide a base level of information to be able to set up deductions, but the balance of keys to deductions is what separates a bad deduction game from a good one. I would say [i]Unheard[/i] errs by being mostly about regurgitating keys. If you had the cases as text transcripts, you'd be able to solve each case almost instantaneously. The English-language DLC is quite a bit better because it actually involves a bunch of piecing together and deduction. There are individual questions and names in a few of the base cases that likewise require deduction. But if you're fresh off [i]Obra DInn[/i], [i]Golden Idol[/i], or [i]Roottrees[/i] and looking for more, this absolutely ain't it chief.

As someone who loves detective and puzzle games, Unheard - Voices of Crime grabbed my interest right away. This mystery game takes a different approach by making you solve crimes through sound alone. You play as a detective who pieces together stories by listening. You're essentially a fly on the wall. You eavesdrop on conversations and pick up environmental sounds to reconstruct the events leading up to a crime.

You're working toward two objectives in every level. First, you need to match voices to the right characters. Second, you answer important questions about the case. You move around the crime scene using a virtual map, and the audio shifts depending on where you position yourself. This means you'll replay the same audio clip several times to catch all the details you need.

The other characters show up as dotted circles on your map. When they talk, you see a visual equalizer effect around them. Once you match names to these circles, you can follow where characters go throughout the scene, even when you're listening from a different room.

Each case is really well crafted and exciting to solve. I found them genuinely satisfying to work through. The cases get more complex as you progress through the five main scenarios (plus additional DLC content). The later cases throw bigger maps at you, along with longer recordings and more characters to track. This makes careful listening really important, and you'll definitely want to take notes. Thankfully, you can add notes directly to the audio timeline, which helps you remember key moments.

I'd recommend using headphones when you play. The audio quality is solid, with background sounds that really pull you into each scene. The voice acting works well overall. Some performances are a bit over the top, but this actually helps you tell characters apart, which matters since the game depends entirely on audio.

One important note: people with hearing difficulties should know the game doesn't include subtitles. This could make it challenging or impossible to play.

Unheard is a short crime-solving game with a neat concept: You can listen in to conversations and interactions that took place shortly before a crime was committed and when you feel ready, you answer a few questions about the crime to solve it. 

Each case (there are five in total) consists of a recording of everything that took place before a crime happened, a list of names and a map of the soon-to-be crime scene. You can only listen to conversations if you are in the same room and you don't know who is speaking, either. Your first task is to assign names from your list to the voices you hear. 
You can either follow around a particular person and listen to all their interactions or stay in a room and observe everything that's happening there. You can go back and forth in time at will and do both. You can even fast-forward the recording to quickly see the movements of yourr person(s) of interest. You can leave timestamps with comments to mark specific events. And slowly but surely you'll get a hopefully complete picture of what happened there. 

The concept is similar to Sexy Brutale which I also liked. Unheard is less "gamified" in a way, you're just an invisible presence, no one can see you and you can't interact with anything. This is pure crime solving by listening for clues and making connections.  

I enjoyed playing Unheard quite a bit, a perfect game to play when you just have an hour to kill. Recommended!

The DLC is a brilliant piece of detective gaming, and it essentially doubles the game time free of charge.

Unheard is a detective game where you deduce the identities of suspects using only dialogue and placement on a floorplan map. The game is about piecing together events and conversations to figure out the logical conclusion as to whodunit and how. The game cleverly manages to make even the early cases not striaghtforward, and consistently throws a loop into the mix to ensure you never have an easy understanding of the full picture. The game's dialogue works well and walking around the floorplan with the tools given to you is satisfying and helpful to solve the cases.

On the other hand, much of the game is sitting and listening to the dialogue play out, and some later levels can be 15 minutes long. I would have liked the fat to be trimmed from some conversations and for the levels to be more compact, but denser in concurrent events. The audio also really messed me up. Playing with headphones, it was never comfortable to listen to an entire conversation because voices severely pan left or right depending on how your character is standing. I understand it's to seem like we are in the room, but it ended up being more distracting than immersive. I wish this was a toggle feature, to just hear the room in proximity rather than in LR.

Overall, I think the game is really well-done, and I hope that the DLC missions get translated so we can get a longer overall game for the price of admission. I'm excited to play the one that does exist as of now. 

Sidenote, i would also love to see someone's take on this concept if it was in 3D, where you can walk around the space and see the rooms.

They won't give it to you.

[i]Unheard[/i] is a 5 hour puzzle game with an interesting storyline. It combines the game mechanics from [i]Tacoma[/i] and [i]Obra Dinn[/i], such that the player can replay events in order to identify the people involved. The gameplay is sufficiently challenging and often requires the player to get intimately familiar with each stage prior to solving it.

The Shanghai-based developer, NEXT Studios, starts off by advising the player to use headphones, priding the game on its auditory mechanics. I, on the other hand, would advise not to use headphones. It's true that the audio and voice acting are central to the game, but the sound engine playing these sounds is incredibly basic. At first I was confused to see my avatar face a sound source while hearing the sound off-center, only to find out the avatar's orientation isn't taken into consideration. Worse, however, is the disregard of environment. Standing to the left of a sound source will result in all audio coming from the right, regardless of the room you're in. This quickly becomes annoying, but luckily it's easily overcome by using speakers.

Overall [i]Unheard[/i] is an interesting game, worth the 5 hours and 4 euros. Plus, it comes with a free 3 hour DLC of the same quality. 7/10

In this game, you visit crime scenes and have to solve a couple of questions they give you based off the audio of the characters involved. I thought the concept sounded really cool. Something I found really neat is how you can visit different rooms and hear different conversations that occur at the same time as others. It really helps piece the mystery together when you're able to hear all perspectives. It's not too difficult but also not that easy, and as someone that struggles with mysteries, I appreciate it a lot. The game is pretty short and I would have liked more, but what you get out of it makes the price tag reasonable at least.

Some minor things I would complain about is the voice acting sometimes had some awkward delivery. [b][u]General Thoughts:[/u][/b]
Unheard is a short but intriguing puzzle/RPG/detective hybrid. The base premise is that you are investigating crimes by moving an avatar around a floorplan and listening in on capture audio to identify people and answer whodunit style questions about the crime. It’s an eavesdropper’s dream, with multiple people and complex storylines that require attention to detail. 

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*]The concept is novel (at least to me) and makes for an interesting gameplay experience.
[*]The missions/scenarios are written well enough that every detail can be important. Entire hypotheses can constructed and demolished in single sentences, with so many players it’s quite possible to be sure of your answers, only to find you’ve missed something that changes everything.
[*]Each mission is short enough that you don’t get bored, but deep enough that there is a lot to unpack and explore. This also feeds into the pacing of the game, with each scenario growing more complex. 
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The voice acting is ham-fisted and extremely over the top. This could actually be intended as a positive, as the stereotypes make for easier identification. 
[*] The overarching story is extremely cringe worthy, poorly written, and frankly, it damned near ruins the experience. The game would have been significantly more satisfying without it.  
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
 [list][*] The scope is really limited with only five scenarios and locked sets of questions / layouts, even having just a few different questions with a random set allocated each time would add a little something to the mix. 
[*] A skip cut scene button.
[*] Better voice acting.
[/list]

[b][u]Overall Recommendation:[/u][/b]
Don’t go into this expecting Doyle or Christie. It’s more cluedo. I think if you’re open to a slightly different puzzle game, or enjoy detective style games, you might get something out of this. It’s short enough to finish in an evening or two, and novel enough to be worth trying out, if its on sale, of course. That said, I give it the old thumbs up.

This is basic game development, come on now. The way they responded to calls for subtitles rubbed me the wrong way, and their rabid fanbase has been quick to defend this boneheaded decision.

I get that they were stoked about their novel game mechanic and subtitles aren’t an inherent part of that mechanic, but hey man, you can just add subtitles and let users that need them worry about that. Trust me when I say you can’t disappoint me, An awful subtitle implementation is better than shrugging and saying well guess it’s not for you, have better hearing next time loser. 

The game should’ve been more clear on the store page that this is a whole lot of ASMR audio, which I absolutely cannot listen to with headphones. ASMR on headphones is creepy and extremely uncomfortable (to me). The voice acting gets better through later cases, but it never sounds totally normal because there’s no background noise, just an ASMR recording in a vacuum.

I have also seen in reviews of other games by this developer that they routinely violate user privacy. Apparently this game is also excessively phoning home to their servers. I haven’t looked into this myself but it’s in the discussion forums. 

The cases themselves were shockingly well made. I didn’t run into any of the harebrained impossible logic that episodic detective games can’t seem to get enough of in later cases. I will give them credit for citing stories and movies they used to create the plots and for sticking to their guns on only putting out high quality english localization. 

I have to give this a Do Not Recommend based on how subtitles were handled and I’d encourage prospective buyers to look into this Developer’s other games (to see how sus they are) before hitting that green button. Look up the delisted game “SYNCED” and read the reviews.

This review is going to be pretty long but I want to give a more technical and critical look at this game than I see most other reviewers are giving for both people who haven't played the game and for those that have finished it. Many reviews give Unheard great praise and high scores which I think the game is deserving of, but I think there is a lot to be improved on here and even if you like conventional mystery/detective games you might be bored with Unheard. Normally I would split my review into a no spoilers section and a spoilers section, however something that can easily be spoiled about this game is what type of mechanics and skills the gameplay includes. If I were to tell you "It sucks that the game never does X" then you will play through the game never taking X into account as a possibility making you confident in some things that you otherwise don't deserve to be confident in. Because of this I will be spiting this review into 3 different sections, one that does not include spoilers for both the story and gameplay, one that includes spoilers for the gameplay but not the story, and one that includes spoilers for everything. If you want to know my overall rating of the game I would give it a 5/10 which I believe is average, since this game executes a fairly fresh concept that's a pretty damn good score and I would love to see NEXT studios improve upon it. 

no story spoiler/no gameplay giveaways section:

Gameplay in Unheard goes as the following. Enter a case and you will be given a list of names of people in that case, task one is matching the names to the identity of the person. Task two is then finding out some secondary information like who planted the bomb, who detonated the bomb, who is the thief. To uncover these secrets you are given the ability to walk around sorta like a ghost and listen to the conversations held between everyone in the case, you can rewind time and you can add comments at points in time.

Unheard Is a game of high ambitions and mixed result. If you are wondering whether or not to buy it I would say try the second case, if you didn't get what you wanted out of the second case you probably wont get it out of the rest of the game so refund it. The game does ramp up in difficulty but it only ramps up in difficulty in the areas of intelligence that it initially ask you to be proficient in. Some things that you can easily praise the game on is it has excellent sound design which is pretty crucial for a game that has you mostly standing and listening. The graphics do their job, they set a decent tone of a dark and confusing environment. With a couple of questionable instances the logic is pretty air tight, However the cases and some of the timing in the game seems very contrived for the sake of complexity. This contrivedness does somewhat make sense in the game near the end but is never justified truly.

no story spoiler/gameplay giveaways:

Mystery/Detective games typically contain certain skills to be able to complete, The skill that I can safely say Unheard does very well at testing Is memory. There will be times when there are up to 14 people in a single case and typically when two characters are talking they might give vital information about another, This makes taking notes and the comment feature very useful tools and the game does well at ramping up the difficulty of this at a normal pace. What I cant praise Unheard on is how it handles logical reasoning. The game feels like a lot of missed opportunities because of this. Imagine a detective game where the initially most obvious guy was always the culprit and where every witness tells you exactly what they saw without trying to deceive you, this is what playing Unheard felt like. Your omnipresence and invisibility makes it so people generally don't have anything to hide from you and the game never gives really gives people a reason to lie to each other, and if it was a lie you figure it out because the person later reveals it to be so, you never catch someone in the act by thinking "No that's impossible because the door should have been locked!" which is personally one of my favorite parts about mystery games. One of my favorite games of all times is Return of the Obra Dinn which i feel like this game probably took inspiration from and in that game identifying people's names is the hardest part of the game. Its a shame that in Unheard, even though applying names to people is a major mechanic, The names are pretty much always blatantly told to you and sometimes in a contrived way. when two unnamed characters walk in a room and a third character goes "John, Stacy, good to see you two!" I don't feel like I earned the ability to knock two unknowns off my list.

Full spoilers:

The story in this game is a mess but in a good way, I think what i got would be what most people describe as the "true ending" to the game and I would like to think that the ambiguity of it is intended by the developer, ironically if this ambiguity of was present in the gameplay Unheard might have been a serious contender for some top 10 mystery game list. While the story is cool and offers this food for thought It's hard to shake the idea that the developer formulated the story and then made the gameplay as a way to improve the story rather than the other way around. The naming mechanic poses no challenge in the actual game but makes for a somewhat cool ending scenario, which leads me to believe that the only reason the naming mechanic was added was to fuel that story moment.

When I played the last case and the game asked me who I was I answered detective. My reasoning for this was as follows, in the last case George forced Maestro to do a similar thing to what the protagonist is doing, going through the cases. When Maestro said he remembered himself being in the case George was disappointed. Georges goal was to brainwash Maestro and Maestro adding himself as a character in the story seemed to somehow halt progress towards that goal. From this the obvious choice would be to insert yourself as a character of the last case so that they cannot brainwash you but I felt a little cheekier than that. George being upset about Maestros decision was part of the system that was brainwashing you, therefore I came to the conclusion that I was being tricked and if I didnt want to get brainwashed I should chose not insert myself as a character in the case and instead just say I was the detective. I chose this option with a smile on my face expecting the interrogator lady to be upset with my decision, being mad like George was at Maestro, then to my surprise I had "past the test" and was allowed to leave, I had done the exact thing the interrogator lady wanted. This leaves me many questions, If answers to these question do exist then I am not smart enough to figure this out myself. These questions would be: Was I brainwashed in the end or did I truly retain my identity, If I was brainwashed than to what level did I get outplayed? Maybe the situation between Geroge and Maestro was trying to be truthful to me and inserting yourself as a character is the trick to prevent brainwashing. Or Maybe the game forsaw me trying to outsmart it by duping it and doing the opposite like I did only for it to double dupe me. In the end I don't know and I think it's fine to keep it open ended like this even though i would particularly enjoy if there was some deductive way to prove the validity of my choice. 

there's a lot more things I would like to talk about like the following: the only time someone lies about their identity is the first case, phone calls not playing interesting roles in the cases, and what the last case defining as "real mental patient" being murky with the brainwashing. And the female cop in the 5th case somehow learning spoon's name when never told. But I am reaching the limit here so please let me know your take on the story, would be interested to get into discussions about it.

Unheard is an audio drama, where you deduce solutions to five different mystery scenarios by listening to up to 12 different characters at a time during scripted events (about 17 minutes for the longest one). You're free to jump between locations - following characters or staying put - and rewind and fast forward as you please. By listening to each character, you'll be able to assign identities to each of them and eventually answer the questions that solve the mystery.

Graphics are simple room layouts and icons representing individual characters. Except for scripted cut scenes between each scenario, it's this simple, but utilitarian representation you'll be looking at. It works fine for what it's supposed to do.

Both the audio and the script is of fairly high quality. I'd say about 90% of the English speaking actors do a good job, but a few give stale or overly dramatic performances. Still, there's nothing truly cringe worthy here, which is obviously important for an audio drama.  Each individual scenario has a decent enough script, delivering a mystery you'll want to solve, and giving you all the tools you need to actually do the solving. Unfortunately, the conclusion to the overarching story is by far the weakest part of the script. I kind of think I'll just pretend it isn't there, really.

Now, the major issue you might have with this, is that there are no subtitles inside the actual scenarios. This means that if you don't have a strong grasp of English (or Chinese), it may be extremely hard for you to complete this. The voice actors are clear and coherent, but if you struggle with the language itself, there isn't any help, other than listening to the same phrase over and over until you get it. As you can imagine, if you miss something important in a detective game, any of the scenarios could suddenly become impossible to solve.

So, fair warning: If you're not confident in your spoken English or Chinese, you should really think twice about getting this. At least until such a time as the developer possibly patches in subtitles.

On the other hand, if you are confident, and you're looking for a fun deduction game, I recommend this. It's cheap, and the developer is apparently planning free DLC for the game in the future, adding to the value of what you already get.

If I had to sum it up in one statement : The idea is amazing, but the execution is lackluster.

- The game doesn't rely much on its main medium to enhance the experience or make it more challenging. The most you can get is the occasional impersonation or picking up on voice tones in calls to figure out whether it's coming from inside the building or outside.
Besides that, the cases are as simple as they can get. All you have to do is be at the right place on the right time, listen, and that's it. No sleuthing or deductions needed.
The only exception being the DLC, because that's the only challenging case in my opinion. But I find its execution to be wack because the 2nd Case is just replaying the first with the addition of one room ... Making it, oh so boring.

- There are no subtitles, and this seems to be a common complaint from what I've gathered from other reviews. And I agree. 
If you're sticking to not including subtitles (hearing impaired individuals be damned), I would expect eloquent voice acting. And this is by no means shade towards the actors themselves, I just find that some deliveries are indiscernible. Again, the DLC did a better job on that front, although not by much. But this would have been prevented if we had access to the Sub ...

- The story is ... Without going into spoiler territory, the execution of the "twist" was weak. Maybe this is more of a translation issue than a writing one due to the game being original in Chinese, but I just find it to be out of nowhere.
The audio cues in the background are not well-made to make the player feel like something is off. If anything, they just add to the atmosphere of being in a room (echo sounds). 
That one line used by the woman you're talking to between case 3 and 4 feels like a throwaway line. You can't build a whole overarching plot twist on one line like that and feel like it ties the entire narrative up.

- The writing for the dialogue leaves a lot to be desired. Again, could be a translation issue, so I can't comment about the native language of the game.

- I have nowhere to add this but the feature for where you leave notes on the audio ? Get rid, or turn it into time stamps that can be clicked on for replay conveniences. No need for what you wrote to fly by the screen the moment you reach its segment.

I don't know. The more I write down my thoughts, the more I get confused about my feelings towards the game. Because, yes, the game is fun regardless of what I wrote above (in fact, I did recommend it to my friends). 
But to an avid mystery game enjoyer or someone who's seeking more detective work ? I don't think this is the game for you. 
And I think I'm leaning towards the latter.

With that aside, I hope that we get other games that build up on this concept. There is enough games that rely on visual clues than audible, and I think there is a lot to explore on this front.

TLDR : 
If you're not hearing impaired and a casual detective game enjoyer ? Feel free to give this a try.
If you're not ? Maybe look for another game.

This game is definitely worth the price tag. Sure it only took 4 hours to complete the game, but a movie costs twice as much, is over in half the time, and is not this immersive. 

If you like "who-dunnit" type games with a government surveillance element, I highly recommend this game. It’s like Orwell without all the reading or Don’t Feed The Monkeys without the distractions. The audio aspect of this game is an impressive twist on the genre.
If you like games like Her Story or other atmospheric investigation games, this is a great game. With just 5 levels very short but gives you some hours to play. Worth to get in every sale.

The gameplay for this was really cool and refreshing. You're basically playing a fly on the wall, listening in on to different conversations in a building. You'll listen to the recording several times, moving yourself to different rooms or following different people each time to get the whole idea of what is going on in the building. It felt kind of like listening to a podcast from multiple perspectives. It was really neat. At the end you need to determine the solution to a number of questions pertaining to what you just witnessed, usually who commit the crime and maybe one or two other things relevant to what you just heard.

There isn't much gameplay aside from following people around, listening to them, marking who each speaker is, and then answering the questions. I know it doesn't sound like much but it was still pretty cool. It's like going over audio security footage and analyzing it. You can also take notes if you feel like you need to. When you're replaying the audio your note will always appear and glide across the screen at the timestamp you wrote it, so it can be a nice refresher to a different conversation going on in the building.

You can probably multitask while playing this game (like doing something on your phone at the same time) but I don't think that takes away from it, I do that with podcasts and still enjoy them.

There are five stories, each audio varying from 4 minutes to 15, but don't forget you'll be listening to them multiple times. There's also a free DLC available which I haven't tried yet. Unfortunately the paid DLC is not localized.

Took me a little over 3 hours to beat, but I see the playtime for many users varies so I might just be good at this kind of thing. I feel like most people will get between 3-5 hours out of it.

Definitely glad I finally got around to playing this.

It's a decent detective game. Still, quite bare-bones and threadbare. It's indie, but the immersive kind. Opposite what the Steam score suggests, people probably should not expect something earth-shattering. Quite enjoyable and there's plenty of variety in the cases. 2D Obra Dinn-lite.

Kinda neat concept. Way too short. Over the top voice acting made it sound goofy. Cases were too easy to solve.

Unheard is a game with an extraordinarily cool concept which is executed basically perfectly but never pushed anywhere close to its limits.

The comparisons to Return of the Obra Dinn are obvious but appropriate, and I will say that Unheard is the only other game to scratch that same you-work-it-out-yourself itch. Like Obra Dinn, [i]you the player[/i] have to make all the logical connections, piecing together the story without any gimmicky framework or guiderails from the game, and that sort of puzzle gameplay is so rare that anybody who liked the former game should definitely give this one a try.

The downside is that the puzzles just never get [i]hard[/i]. Obra Dinn has a few easy deductions, a few medium challenges that require you to coordinate and cross-reference the easier ones, and a few real stumpers that you can't solve unless (again) you the player are actually observant enough of the little details. Unheard never gets to that last level, and rarely dips its toes into the second. There is one really good puzzle in the Theater level (identifying the source of the ghost texts) that requires paying careful attention to sequence and positioning, but pretty much everything else can be solved just by listening to every conversation once and recording all the details when they are spoken out loud.

In other words, my biggest frustration is that the game doesn't push its systems [i]enough[/i] -- there is so much potential left on the table here that I was actually brainstorming other puzzle ideas after I finished the relatively short campaign. Still a strong recommendation to anybody who likes deductive reasoning, but don't get your hopes up for any brain-busting puzzles.

The concept is solid. Walking around, getting to eavesdrop on past events to solve crimes is immediately enticing. It's too bad that it just doesn't come together at all. 

I can't speak to how this game is in Chinese. I only played it in English, but the English voice acting was simply bad. This wouldn't normally be something I'd spend too much time on but considering the entire game is listening to people acting, it's pretty painful. Nearly every character sounds like someone doing a bad stereotype rather than a normal human's voice. By the time I rolled credits, I wasn't surprised to see nearly every actor pulling double duty (and often far more) but frankly, I was surprised to see as many actors as there were. There was a while where I legitimately thought every masculine voice was the same actor.

Then there's the story. Frankly, there isn't one. Each of the five cases is entirely standalone except for one of them which links up for no particular reason. The plot point doesn't go anywhere and frankly, they would have been better off just keeping each one self-contained rather than trying to shoehorn in a link with no real purpose since that just disappointed us more. None of the cases are particularly interesting and none do anything all that interesting with the premise either. You may think that the game will try to use the fact that you can only hear the scenes to trick you but no, not really. There's one small instance where this comes up but if you just listen to another character, they'll spell out what's actually going on. No thinking required and no engagement with the plot is needed. 

But what about the deductions? Each case will have you assign names to each of the figures and then answer a couple of questions about the situation. There isn't a single name in this game that can't be learned by just following that person around long enough for someone to say their name, which is always correct, or through basic process of elimination. Did that woman not get a name? Just wait until it's the only feminine name left in the name bank and you'll have it. The questions are often even easier. One case in particular, we only listened through once, following only the person we started next to, and despite feeling like we didn't really know what was going on, we knew the answers to the questions so we opted to just answer them and move on. None of the questions really make you deduce anything so much as they just want you to listen to the right person at the right time and apply a tiny amount of common sense.

Unheard, simply put, is a great idea and nothing more. The cases aren't interesting. The framing story goes nowhere and the cases aren't linked in any interesting ways. The deductions are dead simple and can often be solved without a full understanding of the case. Notetaking would be a waste of your time. The acting is painfully bad. Even for $7, I can't recommend this when there are so many incredible deduction games coming out on Steam all the time.
Great game, where you use your ears to identify people and gather information. Very Innovative, I just wish the game was longer, cause it's such an interresting idea.

It’s safe to say that I have never played anything remotely similar to Unheard. It`s quite short but still enjoyable and full of engaging content. The English voice actors are simply the best – I don’t care about what other reviewers say. I think the voice actors did a fair job and deserve some praise. They were super articulate and easy to understand for a non-native speaker so I was satisfied with their work overall. The writing of the game is mesmerizing and demands lots of attention from players.  The main branch of the game has five scenarios and you can rewind time in order to eavesdrop on the conversation between characters in different rooms or places etc.  It’s not the hardest detective game I’ve played (there were some confusing moments and red herrings but nothing impossible to understand) but the most innovative and unique one - that’s for sure. Apart from the main branch the game also has some DLCs but most (except for one) haven’t been translated into English. And it seems that they won’t be translated at all so you might as well start learning Chinese if you want to get more content from Unheard. (They successfully translated the main game but can't do the same for their dlcs? Seems a bit off to me. My best guess is that the community consists mainly of Japanese and Chinese folks and developers do not really care about English speaking lads because there aren’t a lot of them here. Honestly, such a shame but what can we do. Let’s hope that they translate the DLCs into English one day.
solid puzzles that are very satisfying to resolve. if any more of the dlc gets localized to english i will definitely be buying it

This is a pretty unique detective game around the concept of listening to various conversations between different characters around the same time in order to piece together the narrative. 

I got pretty immersed in the game so I was disappointed when I found out some stuff about the game. While the game is a decent fun time it's far from perfect and sadly has some flaws, Firstly the game is surprisingly short which isn't a deal breaker by any means as each case is an interesting string of webs as you try to piece together the narrative in order to help solve the mysteries layed out in front of you but it does end up leaving you wanting more. The game contains roughly 5 individual cases assuming you count the free DLC after launch along with the base game which makes that 6 but even that feels a bit generous since the first case that serves as the game's tutorial is fairly short imo especially in comparison to the rest of the cases in the game that could roughly take as long as 30 or 40 minutes to an hour long depending on how good your detective skills are.

Secondly, not all the questions but some of them presented during each case are a bit hit or miss in their execution. They're either unintentionally leading or a bit too vague at times although this was probably a side effect of this being translated from the devs native tongue to english so I can't blame the devs as it's already hard enough to make as indepth and interesting stories for a detective game that can keep me engaged throughout as Unheard has and on top of that having to translate it to other languages can make things alot more convoluted and difficult to manage.

Apart from those issues it's a great time. The narratives are pretty interesting to watch unfold and that's made even better by the acting, while it can be a bit cheesy at times and some of the executions of some lines by characters weren't always up to snuff the actors who worked on this game did a pretty damn good job so if you're interested in playing a fresh take on a detective game then I highly recommend this although if you're slightly put off by the idea of spending money on a game as short as this then you can always wait for it to go on sale. I hope this helps :D

The main premise of this game is that you are a detective attempting to solve cases. However the unique part is that you are only given a floor plan and complete a complete audio stream of what happened in the minutes leading up to the crime. You'll have to accurately deduce which character is which just by listening in on their conversations, and solve several key question related to the case.
Simply following one or two people won't provide you with the full context to what happened so you'll need to follow most if not all of the characters to find all of your answers.
It's an interesting premise and it is quite fun to figure out the story piece by piece, as you hear a new part of the conversation that completely changes the context of what you've already heard.

There are two main criticisms I have of the game though. First, the game is pretty short. The playtime only clocks in at a few hours, and there's little incentive to return once you've already heard everything there is to hear.
Second is that the difficulty is fairly low. In most cases just about everyone will have their name said loudly by their conversation partner so it's really just busywork filling it out. I feel that there could have been more clever indirect ways to reveal a characters identity. Although, there were a couple of key questions that did force me to think a bit, even after I had heard it all.

Overall, it's a fairly nice experience. It might be worth waiting on a sale though. I have heard that the dev plans on releasing more content that is more challenging with at least some of it being free, so hopefully it will remedy the issues I have with this game.

Disclaimer that I've only played the base game, not the DLCs. 

This is one of those cases where the lack of nuances in Steam reviews gets in the way of a good evaluation.

This is a 5.5/10 for me, but I'd find it unfair to give it a negative review. The game is fine, you can solve the 5 cases that come with the base game with relative ease in less than 4 hours and I'd say it's fun for its whole duration. 
Problem is the real game is not solving the cases, but correctly matching the names with the voices - once you do that, you can brute-force the actual answers to the crimes and that's it. The whole atmosphere of the game tries to convince you that something creepy is or will happen, but without much substance. You finish the game with a feeling of "that's it?". Also, the achievements don't make much sense - why would I torture myself by not using the fast-forward option in a 13-minute clip I've been listening to for the 4th time?

I've found other detective games, such as Return of the Obra Dinn and The Case of the Golden Idol, way more enjoyable. Either way, Unheard still deserves some respect for trying - and partially succeding - to give a new approach to the genre. If you're looking for some quick detective fun, this game will do it. I'd recommend to only buy it on a sale tho.

Fantastic game! It is a work picking detective game but you need to move around a map, identify all characters and listen to their stories going on to answer some queries.  Generally, who is the killer and then unique questions.  5 levels and free DLC level, well worth the money for a chilled evening.
If you like detective games, add this to the top of the list

Unheard is a game that I liked a lot more than I thought I would. At it's core, the game is a detective mystery, in which you are given a room layout and a timeline, and you have to figure out who did a crime, and why. 

For this, you can jump to any moment in time leading up to the crime, walk into an area, and listen to the audio that has been audible in that space during that time. Slowly, you start to piece together what happened, why it happened, and who is responsible. 

What works great about this, is that the 5 mysteries that you have to solve are incredibly complex - every person in the scene usually has some sort agenda. People lie, betray each other, and unplanned things happen, so it takes some caution to draw conclusions. The last one even ambitiously ties all of the previous stories together in a way that actually works really well. Narratively, this game is really ambitious, and can actually pull it off. 

I have some smaller nitpicks about the game, namely, that it can sometimes be annoying to listen through the entire level - the last level is 15 minutes of recording and features 12 characters, which means that you probably spend over an hour just listening to all of the interactions happening in the scene. Also, listening to all of the audio already concludes 80% of the investigation. It still feels *good* to figure out all of the intrigue, but a lot of it is actually still just being told to you. But the other 20% are very cool, because the game doesn't hold your hand in drawing your own conclusions at all. Additionally, the game's questions about the case actually spoiled a plot twist in one instance, which I found a bit sad. 

I think this is a great game to experience narratively, but if you are looking for something where you can sink your teeth in to solve a case that is really hard to crack, this might not be the best game for you. I *really* enjoyed playing it, though. The levels all felt super unique, the game was short enough to not wear out it's mechanics, and it's just a super creative idea in general!

The game's not horrible, the concept's neat and overall there's definitely a few enjoyable gocha moments. There are however 2 large issues with it. Mild spoilers ahead but nothing that would make the game worse to experience.

[olist]
[*]The entirety of the challenge comes from simply not jumping to conclusions until you heard the entire 40 minutes worth of audio clips from over 12 different perspectives, as once you've listened to everything figuring out what happened is trivial. Too little is left to guesswork.
[*]The endings sour the experience. I honestly don't know why they went for this spoopy, cryptic, meta, up to your interpretation ending but it really clashes with the rest of the game that's all about deducing the truth.
[/olist]

A few other nitpicks off the top of my head:
[list]
[*]Your character moves entirely too slowly, the only reason for not having a simple pointer on where to listen sound from is the ending.
[*]The controls and comment systems are bare-bones, you need to constantly rewind to a specific point to read your comments from a specific time. Hover to view would have been much better. But it's not like the comments are very useful anyway. On top of that there's just no way to speed up the listening process, if the game offered a visualized audio track below where you can see where the majority of talking is happening for each room, looking for info would be immensely easier.
[*]The game would have benefited greatly from more hectic, compact, complicated situations. A 3-4 minute long file with 30 perspectives that constantly interject each-other.
[*]Too much hand-holding. A character standing at the door or running around, naming most of the cast ruins the detectivework of figuring out who's who. 
[/list]

Ultimately, I can't recommend this game with a clear conscience. Just go play "The Return of the Obra Dinn" if you want to solve a complex mystery from only a handful of clues.

An interesting premise, great audio and some interesting stories. I enjoyed all the layers to each, where you may initially make one assumption then have it flipped on its head after following another person's perspective. This game had some potential. Then the final level was a mental hospital and it devolved into a pile of weak and stigmatising tropes, which then follow to a truly uninspired ending that felt like it was trying too hard to be edgy. No thanks.

Played this in one sitting. Fantastic game. Recommend for people who love a good mystery and who are good at deduction. Would not recommend to anyone who has a hard time with audio processing. 

As an auditory learner, this game was right up my alley. My only complaint is that I want more.
This is honestly one of the best games I've played in a long time. It's short, but it makes your think and question things. It's also so original with a great twist! Absolutely 10 out of 10

This game is pretty fun! The concept is pretty unique and it's executed well overall. The game initially got harder and more complex. The museum case was my favorite, followed by the police station one. I thought overall they did a good job challenging you by not dropping names as easily, but in the last two cases they felt a little more like they were holding your hand. I don't see any other reviews mentioning this, but the framing device is kind of spooky, which I didn't anticipate but was still intriguing.  There are enough other schemes that are going on throughout the case that you can follow through and figure out what's going on, even if it doesn't end up being relevant to the questions you need to answer.  The voice acting is pretty good. Overall, I'd definitely recommend it! I'd love another game like this or a DLC.

I really like this game, but jeez it's less than an hour and a half of content. It's fun untangling the mysteries, they did a decent job making events confusing, it really comes down to being in the right room at the right time. Really wish there was more of it. Also the ending is a bit garbage, comes out of nowhere and you can't know what to do because there's been zero indication what's coming. It's like they had this ending in mind, but then forgot to build it into the rest of the game. Or I suspect there were more missions planned which would haven't brought the ending together, but they decided to release without finishing all that. Also the achievements to "Pass [mission number here] without fast-forwarding and rewinding" makes no sense, I got a few of them despite using the rewind, it's probably a translation error.

5 mysteries (1 tutorial, 4 full length)
Playtime approximate 3.5 hours

Easy to moderate deductive level requiring 1 or 2 step thinking

Good writing and sound

Unique and interesting idea, but the execution is incredibly dull. The major pain points are 

1) the writing is incredibly amateurish and intentionally generic. 

2) The acting and delivery is so slow, and the game offers no ability to change the playback speed (e.g. 2.0x) 

3) By design, you have to listen to the audio multiple times, but the scrubbing tools are non-existent. The re-listening is an interesting idea, but 1) and 2) make it insufferable.


The game would be much, much better if it offered the ability to adjust the playback speed (e.g. 2.0x) so it didn't feel like the entire thing was a waste of time.

The fact that the DLC explicitly makes fun of its own poor casting in the very last part is quite fitting for a game that has such poor voice acting. Does it count as self-irony or is it a cheap way to rationalize and justify the lack of quality? I guess both.

In general,  'Unheard' revolves around listening to people's conversations in person or on the phone and find out who is who and whodunnit. Self-referential plots and brain twisting scenarios abound.

Recommended, with caveats, for surveillance enthusiasts.

Unheard is another deductive detective game in the growing genre inspired by Return of the Obra Dinn. You are a detective cross-referencing audio conversations to solve crimes. The deductions are decently executed, but the overall low quality of the execution lets it down.

For a game composed primarily of spoken audio, the voice-acting quality is quite poor. The mechanic to "lock in" correct guesses is more crude and less satisfying that its peers.

I would only recommend this game if you're desperate for another taste of that sweet sweet deductive gameplay.

In this game you are a detective that has to solve cases just by listening to video recordings. it starts simple but gets complicated quickly.
the UI is very simple and the controls are easy to understand. you can take notes ingame to keep track of everything that's happening.
the recordings are very long and you have to listen to them multiple times to get the viewpoints of different characters. but that doesnt make it boring, since every character does something else in a scene so you hear something new.
only negative thing that I can think of is, that it unfortunately has no subtitles and the audio is in English, making it not accessible for everyone.

I don't recommend this game to anyone who expects good (voice) acting or non-stereotypical characters. Instead, most of the lines are pronounced in a cartoonish way and there was [b]no attempt at all[/b] to make the characters feel real people. I think it's OK for those players who think that super-emphatic acting is acceptable for narrating dramatic events, but for me it makes all the scenes feel fake and breaks my suspension of disbelief.

It's hard to explain why you should try this game without actually giving away anything. It's like trying to convince a friend to watch a good movie, just telling them that the plot twist at the end is amazing ... kinda gives away the fact that the plot twist exists

Playing it is like getting ready for TOEFL listening test.
for me, it is an easy 7/10

This game is groundbreakingly innovative. The mysteries were complex and very well written, and just using sound and location is a stroke of genius. All puzzle lovers need to get this game, ASAP.

A novel idea whos execution makes it get old very quickly. Maybe its the fault of the localization, but the voice acting and text are giving big "community theater" energy. The voices and accents are very broad to the point of being laughable. Another reviewer was spot-on when they aid it sounds like a radio play. But  the problem is it's a very poor radio made using the vernacular of the 1940s. Which makes it come off like a Looney Tunes gangster cartoon rather than a serious crime story.

I feel like the mechanics are very interesting, but the story didn't make a whole lot of sense. It lost me big time at the mental hospital. 

I know this is from another country, and there might be translation issues, but there is a lot of plot holes. There are a lot of unanswered questions -- not out of creativity but sloppy writing. I'm not sure I understand how any of the cases deal with each other, and what the TAT was? The explanation was quite confusing. 

SPOILER:

Insanity isn't interesting, dramatic, or exciting. It's haunting, miserable, and traumatic for whoever has severe mental health issues. I feel like if any research was done in mental hospitals and the disorders talked about in the game, not only would the game make more sense, but be significantly more informative. 

For example, if Nellie wasn't a "real" patient why would they give her a bed and paper? With this being a fake mental hospital, it's very hard to figure out what the rules and regulations of the mental hospital is. I am assuming the mental hospital is fake because:

-They'd never do the TAT test. Especially in modern times.
-There would be no ash tray in the interrogation room because all sharp objects aren't allowed in mental hospitals
-Again, they gave Nellie a bed and paper even though she wasn't a "real" patient.
-They don't put you in mental hospitals for having selective mutism. They only put you in if your a danger to others or yourself
-Maybe it's different in where the game was made, but it's impossible to escape through windows in mental hospitals.

Us just kind of being "insane" at the end also cuts trust from the player. None of what we played was real, so what was the point, really? It feels like they made the game extremely confusing to seem very well written, but it wasn't. At the end, it just didn't make sense.

This game was really cool. Having to actually listen and pay attention to all the conversations, movements of characters, and other sounds was a nice change of pace. And solving each crime scene was extremely satisfying, because your understanding what's going on evolves over time. Fairly short, but absolutely worth it for the price. I'd love to play any sequels in the same style if they ever made them.

This game was so much fun, the ending definitely through me for a complete loop but I highly recommend this game if you enjoy true crime or if you enjoy the games that make you think. It does need more content because it is a short game, was able to complete all the accomplishments and the dlc in just over 10hrs. I would play this for 100 if there was more content to it. All in all was a fantastic game!

Just completed the game after 8 hours, and I honestly am happy with the price/hours paid ratio. Each of those 8 hours entranced me in a way most games don't. There's no mindlessness in this game. It's pure audio puzzle and is definitely it's own genre.

Quick pros: Easy to play. Captivating. Not demanding on your computer. Original concept. And probably more I can't think of.
Quick cons: Sometimes voice acting needs work but it doesn't hurt the experience much. Micro stutter sometimes in the audio. Dunno what caused it. Wish the end of the audio didn't force you to restart at the beginning. Would like to rewind like any other time.

In Depth Pros: The Comment System. I really liked the comment system and would love for the Devs to really integrate it more deeply in the future! In most puzzle games, you are given the pieces and have to figure out how to put them into place. In Unheard, creating comments was like making my own puzzle pieces and watching them fall into place. When I'd comment that so and so was making a phone call, and watch my previous comment scroll across the screen saying that such and such was receiving a phone call, I made those puzzle pieces and I watched how they fit. I really wanted to see how one interaction at one time affected others in the scene and really wish there was more clever integration of using that comment system to make your own pieces and watch them fit. Because it's amazing when it happens.

Real motives and original characters. You get a really good understanding of what roll each character plays in their scenes. Who this person is and why they do what they do. It's not just basic nonsense to get the player to find the next clue. Each character has a personality and you can figure that out to help guide you along the narrative.

A game for the non-gamer. You don't have to have quick wits or sharp reflexes to solve these puzzles. I'm sure I could get my grandma interested in this game because it's so friendly on the player. It's not mindless, there really is a challenge where you may think one thing, follow a character and realize "Oh! It's not what I thought!" and re-evaluate the situation. It's so unique to play at your own pace and the game doesn't punish you for taking as long as you want to handle each scene.

There aren't many cons to this game that couldn't just be patched out, but here are some that don't pull you away from the experience.

In Depth Cons: The achievements. Not that big of a deal, but most of the achievements are to solve a case without rewinding or fast forwarding and I just feel that is like asking the player to play the game without playing the game. I don't like the idea of being given tools and then be asked not to use them.

Characters know things they shouldn't. There were a few times that I noticed some characters knew the name or activity of another character when it was never revealed to them. Like they just knew that person's name even though they never met and s/he never said it. Or when someone knew what room someone else went into but never witnessed it. Unheard is a Detective simulation game, where you are the Detective, and you get the chance to be a Acoustic Detective, who don't have to be on the crime scene, and talk every suspect, you can be in the middle of events. You get a tablet, and you are good to go!

Let's talk about the visuals, which looks minimalistic. This is not a bad verb for it, because it looks really nice and fit's for this game. Also the whole UI looks nice and the "cutscenes" are well made. I'm really suprised about that.

The game recommends you to use headphones. Because of this, sound "visualization" is on point, also voice volume to distance works perfectly, and also you can hear if there is a door between the character speaking and you. Music is thrilling, makes the whole game like a real detective movie. Sounds works perfect in this game.

Controls is one of the best thing in the game... because you just have to use your mouse. Mouse to control your character, mouse to answer question, mouse to manipulate the time in scenes, you got everything with one device. Easy to use!

Time to talk about the gameplay! So, you are a detective who investigating different cases, where you are in the scene. You can watch events from "your" point of you, which means you are free to go on the place. However, because you are in the scene, you can't hear everything from everywhere, only where you at. You can't interact with the people and surroundings in these scenarios, you just a spectator. Worry nothing, you can always replay or rewind / fast forward the scene on the tablet.Cases are not that hard, if you used to detective stories, but don't thing this is an easy game. You have to listen and watch carefully. 

Your objectives in these case, is to answer the question(s) about the case and find out which voice is which character. This is not always an easy task to do, especially in the DLC case. To answer questions, you just need to give a name, so it's not that difficult to give to the game. 

I loved the gameplay. I listened every dialogue I could, and I enjoyed every story. Some of them are bit silly, but there are dark ones too. Sometimes finding the answers is not easy, and the game only helps you, when you are submiting your answers, and it just only says how many of your answers are correct. You are only able to proceed, if you answered all question correctly, and give the correct names to their voices.

This game is a hidden gem! I'm so happy I bought it, and I finally tried it out. No wonder this game got so positive reviews. It's exciting to play, if you into dialouges and detective stories. It's not action packed, but if you like good stories and also think out of box and get suprised, this game is for you. Also it has multiple endings, however achiving them is not that difficult, but it's still amazing! This game for 5,69€ is all right. You get 5+1 stories, and you can playthrough the game in 4 and half hours if you take your time and look into it's universe. I defintely recommed this gem!
